command: for i in {1..5}; do echo "Item $i"; done
title: For loop iteration
description: Iterate over a list of values, a range, or command output — the foundation of repetitive task automation in bash scripts.

breakdown.meaning: Loop variable i iterates from 1 to 5
Start of loop body
Print current item number
End of loop body

example: for i in {1..3}; do echo "Server-$i is starting..."; done
output:
Server-1 is starting...
Server-2 is starting...
Server-3 is starting...
tip: Use 'for f in *.log; do' to iterate files. Prefer 'while read line' for processing large files line-by-line to avoid word splitting issues.

title: Conditional file check
description: Conditionally execute commands based on exit codes, string comparisons, file tests, or numeric expressions.

breakdown.meaning: Start conditional block
Test if file exists and is a regular file
Execute following commands if condition is true
End of if block

example: if [ -f /etc/hosts ]; then echo 'Hosts file found'; else echo 'Not found'; fi
tip: Use [[ ]] instead of [ ] in bash — it supports regex matching with =~, handles empty variables safely, and avoids word splitting. Always quote variables inside [ ].

command: cat access.log | grep 'POST' | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
title: Pipeline: Top IP addresses
description: Chain commands with pipes to find the top 10 IP addresses making POST requests in an access log.

breakdown.meaning: Read the log file
Filter only POST request lines
Extract the first field (IP address)
Sort IPs alphabetically (required for uniq)
Count consecutive duplicate lines
Sort numerically in reverse (highest first)
Show only top 10 results

example: cat /var/log/nginx/access.log | grep 'POST' | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
tip: Use 'grep -c' for simple counting. This pipeline pattern works for any log analysis task.

command: deploy() { echo "Deploying $1 to $2"; ssh $2 "cd /app && git pull && systemctl restart $1"; }
title: Define a reusable function
description: Define a reusable block of commands that can be called by name, accept arguments via $1 $2, and return an exit code.

breakdown.meaning: Define function named 'deploy'
First argument (service name)
Second argument (server address)
Execute commands on remote server

example:
greet() { echo "Hello, $1! Today is $(date +%A)"; }
greet "DevOps Engineer"
output: Hello, DevOps Engineer! Today is Tuesday
tip: Use 'local' for all variables inside functions to avoid polluting the global scope. Functions return exit codes (not values) — capture output with result=$(my_func).

title: Variable substitution
description: Use parameter expansion to transform variable values, apply defaults for unset variables, and manipulate strings directly in bash.

breakdown.meaning: Assign the string 'DevOps' to variable name
Convert value to lowercase (bash 4+)
Use 'default_value' if UNSET_VAR is unset or empty
Convert value to uppercase (bash 4+)
Substring extraction: first 3 characters

flags.description: Use default if VAR is unset or empty
Assign default if VAR is unset or empty
Use alt value only if VAR is set and non-empty
Print error and exit if VAR is unset or empty

tip: Use ${VAR:?"VAR is required"} at the top of scripts to enforce required environment variables and fail fast with a clear message.

command: trap 'echo "Cleaning up temp files..."; rm -f /tmp/myapp_*' EXIT ERR
title: Signal handling
description: Register cleanup actions that run automatically when the script exits or encounters an error, ensuring resources are always released.

breakdown.meaning: Built-in command to register signal handlers
Commands to execute when the signal is caught
Trigger on any script exit (normal or abnormal)
Trigger when any command returns a non-zero exit code

flags.description: Fires when the shell or script exits for any reason
Fires when a command exits with non-zero status
Reset a signal handler to its default behavior

example:
#!/bin/bash
tmpfile=$(mktemp /tmp/deploy.XXXXXX)
trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"; echo "Temp file removed."' EXIT
echo "Working with $tmpfile"
echo "deploy_status=success" > "$tmpfile"
cat "$tmpfile"
output:
Working with /tmp/deploy.a3fK92
deploy_status=success
Temp file removed.
tip: Always use trap EXIT in scripts that create temp files, lock files, or mount resources. Combine with 'set -e' so ERR traps catch failures early.

command:
cat <<EOF > config.yml
app:
  name: myservice
  port: 8080
EOF
title: Here document
description: Write multi-line content to a file or pass it to a command using a here document, with support for variable interpolation.

breakdown.meaning: Concatenate and output text
Start here document with EOF as the delimiter
Redirect the output into config.yml
Multi-line content with variable expansion
End of here document (must be on its own line, no leading whitespace)

flags.description: Here document with variable expansion enabled
Here document with variable expansion disabled (literal content)
Here document that strips leading tabs (for indented scripts)
Here string: pass a single string as stdin

example:
HOST="db-primary"; PORT=5432
cat <<EOF > /tmp/db-config.yml
database:
  host: ${HOST}
  port: ${PORT}
  pool_size: 10
EOF
cat /tmp/db-config.yml
tip: Use <<'EOF' (single quotes around delimiter) to prevent variable expansion when writing literal scripts or configs that contain $ characters.

command: arr=("a" "b" "c"); for item in "${arr[@]}"; do echo "$item"; done
title: Array operations
description: Create and iterate over indexed arrays in bash for managing lists of servers, services, or configuration values.

breakdown.meaning: Declare an indexed array with three elements
Expand to all array elements
Iterate over each element safely (quoting preserves spaces)
Print each element on its own line

flags.description: All elements (each as separate word when quoted)
All elements as a single string
Number of elements in the array
Append an element to the array

example:
servers=("web-1" "web-2" "db-1")
echo "Total servers: ${#servers[@]}"
for srv in "${servers[@]}"; do
  echo "Pinging $srv..."
done
output:
Total servers: 3
Pinging web-1...
Pinging web-2...
Pinging db-1...
tip: Always double-quote array expansions ("${arr[@]}") to handle elements with spaces correctly. Use associative arrays (declare -A) for key-value pairs.

command: case "$1" in start) echo "Starting...";; stop) echo "Stopping...";; *) echo "Usage: $0 {start|stop}";; esac
title: Case statement
description: Pattern-match on a variable to handle multiple branches cleanly, commonly used in init scripts and CLI argument parsing.

breakdown.meaning: Match the first argument against patterns
Pattern to match the literal string 'start'
End of this case branch (like break)
Default/wildcard pattern (matches anything)
End of case block (case spelled backward)

flags.description: Exact string match for a branch

tip: Case statements are cleaner than long if/elif chains. Use pattern| syntax to handle aliases like prod|production in the same branch.

title: Command substitution
description: Capture the output of a command into a variable using $() syntax, allowing you to use command results in strings, conditionals, or further processing.

breakdown.meaning: Execute the command inside and capture its stdout
Fetch URL silently (no progress bar)
Store captured output in the variable 'result'
Use the captured value in a string

flags.description: Legacy backtick syntax (avoid: hard to nest)
Capture output and check for failure

example:
current_date=$(date +%Y-%m-%d)
hostname=$(hostname -s)
load=$(uptime | awk -F'average:' '{print $2}')
echo "Report for $hostname on $current_date"
echo "Load: $load"
tip: Always prefer $() over backticks. $() nests cleanly and is easier to read. Combine with || to handle command failures gracefully.

title: Test expressions
description: Use [[ ]] test expressions to check file attributes, compare strings, and chain conditions with logical operators for safe scripting.

breakdown.meaning: Test if /path exists and is a directory
Logical AND: run next command only if previous succeeded
Test if /path is writable by the current user
Prints only if both tests pass

flags.description: True if FILE exists and is a regular file
True if DIR exists and is a directory
True if FILE exists and is not empty
True if STRING is empty (zero length)

example:
LOG_DIR="/var/log/myapp"
if [[ -d "$LOG_DIR" ]] && [[ -w "$LOG_DIR" ]]; then
  echo "Log directory is ready"
elif [[ ! -d "$LOG_DIR" ]]; then
  echo "Creating log directory..."
  mkdir -p "$LOG_DIR"
else
  echo "ERROR: $LOG_DIR exists but is not writable"
  exit 1
fi
tip: Prefer [[ ]] over [ ] in bash scripts. [[ ]] supports regex (=~), glob matching, and does not require quoting variables to prevent word splitting.

title: I/O redirection
description: Redirect standard output and standard error to files or combine them, essential for logging, background jobs, and silencing noisy commands.

breakdown.meaning: Any command whose output you want to redirect
Redirect stdout (fd 1) to out.log, overwriting it
Redirect stderr (fd 2) to the same destination as stdout (fd 1)

flags.description: Redirect stderr to wherever stdout is going
Redirect both stdout and stderr to file (bash shorthand)
Append both stdout and stderr to file

example:
echo "=== Deploy started at $(date) ===" > /var/log/deploy.log
./deploy.sh >> /var/log/deploy.log 2>&1
status=$?
echo "=== Deploy finished with code $status ===" >> /var/log/deploy.log
tail -3 /var/log/deploy.log
output:
=== Deploy started at Sat Mar 15 10:30:00 UTC 2025 ===
Pulling latest code... done.
=== Deploy finished with code 0 ===
tip: Order matters: '2>&1 > file' is NOT the same as '> file 2>&1'. The latter is correct for capturing both streams. Use &> as a shorter alternative in bash.

title: While loop
description: Execute a block of commands repeatedly while a condition is true — commonly used for reading files line-by-line or polling until a condition changes.
command: while read -r line; do echo "$line"; done < file.txt

breakdown.meaning: Read each line from input into $line
The body of the loop
Redirect file as input to the loop

flags.description: Read a line without interpreting backslashes

example:
while read -r line; do
  echo "$line"
done < file.txt

# Infinite loop with break
while true; do
  read -rp "Enter value: " val
  [[ "$val" == "quit" ]] && break
done
output:
line one
line two
line three
tip: Use 'while IFS= read -r line; do ... done < file' to safely read files — IFS= preserves leading whitespace and -r prevents backslash interpretation.

title: String manipulation
description: Manipulate strings using bash parameter expansion — extract substrings, strip prefixes/suffixes, and perform substitutions without spawning external tools.

breakdown.meaning: Remove shortest prefix match from start of $var
Remove shortest suffix match from end
Replace first occurrence of old with new

tip: Use ${var:-default} to provide a fallback if var is unset. Use ${var//old/new} for global substitution without calling sed.

title: Arithmetic operations
description: Perform integer arithmetic directly in bash using (( )) or $(( )) — avoids spawning expr or bc for simple calculations.

breakdown.meaning: Arithmetic expansion — evaluates and substitutes the result
Standard arithmetic with operator precedence

example:
x=10
y=3
echo $(( x + y ))    # 13
echo $(( x * y ))    # 30
echo $(( x / y ))    # 3  (integer division)
echo $(( x % y ))    # 1  (modulo)

# Increment
(( x++ ))
echo $x              # 11

# Conditional check
(( x > 5 )) && echo "big"
tip: Use (( )) for conditional arithmetic: 'if (( count > 0 ))'. Use $(( )) for assignment: 'total=$(( a + b ))'. For floats, use awk or bc.

title: Read user input
description: Read user input interactively or line-by-line from a file or pipe — the primary way to make scripts interactive or process streams.

breakdown.meaning: Read a line from standard input
Raw mode — do not interpret backslashes
Display a prompt string before reading
Variable to store the input

example:
read -rp "Enter name: " name
echo "Hello, $name"

# Silent password input
read -rsp "Password: " pass
echo
echo "Got password (length ${#pass})"
tip: Always use 'read -r' to prevent backslash interpretation. Use '-s' for silent input (passwords). Set IFS= before read to preserve leading/trailing whitespace.

title: Exit codes and error handling
description: Every command returns an exit code: 0 means success, non-zero means failure — bash scripts use these to control flow and signal errors to callers.

breakdown.meaning: Exit immediately if any command returns non-zero
Treat unset variables as errors
Fail if any command in a pipe fails

example:
set -euo pipefail

# Check exit code manually
if ! cp src.txt dest.txt; then
  echo "Copy failed" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Trap errors
trap 'echo "Error on line $LINENO"' ERR

# Run command, ignore failure
rm file.txt || true
tip: Add 'set -e' at the top of scripts to exit immediately on any error. Use 'set -o pipefail' so pipes propagate failures — without it, 'false | true' exits 0.
